newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German union sets ultimatum over sick pay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German union sets ultimatum over sick pay.

text.p: German engineering union IG Metall on Thursday began top-level talks with employers hinting at compromise on a bitter dispute over sick pay but threatening industrial action if no deal is reached.

Klaus Zwickel, head of the powerful IG Metall engineering union, said the two sides must find common ground over a new law allowing sick pay to be cut to 80 percent of normal wages from 100 percent currently.
If not, Germany would face a further day of walkouts and protests in the key enginering sector on October 24.
"We are sticking with (our demand for) 100 percent sick pay," Zwickel said as he arrived at a Frankfurt hotel for talks with the engineering employers' association Gesamtmetall.
Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe reaffirmed his commitment to a law aimed at cutting sick pay allowances to 80 percent.
"I couldn't imagine the unions could offer so much that we would move away from this point," Stumpfe told journalists,
The sick-pay cut was backed up by legislation, he said, and as a result should be implemented.

Earlier this week, Gesamtmetall was humiliatingly forced to climb down from its initial firm position on the sick pay issue after walkouts at some of Germany's largest companies disrupted production and caused losses worth millions of marks.
The union promised to suspend its protests in return for the assurance that firms would reverse their decisions to implement the sick pay cut without delay.
Yet ahead of Thursday's talks, both sides hinted they were ready to look at possible compromises.
Leaders of the IG Metall trade union said they would notm move on the central sick pay issue, but added that other concessions on labour costs were now possible.
IG Metall deputy chairman Walter Riester said the union would still seek a nationally-binding clause protecting sick pay at the current level of 100 percent of wages.
"That could also have a price for our side," Riester conceded in Thursday's "Hamburger Abendblatt" paper.

In contrast to the forceful rhetoric that accompanied more than 100,000 metal workers in walkouts last week, other union leaders suggested that some out-of-date work regulations could be revised to cut costs.

"We could also discuss some of those framework regulations that came into being 10 years ago but are possibly not valid today," Gerhard Zambelli, regional IG Metall union leader in the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg, told German television.
Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe, echoed the more conciliatory tone.

"We must find a compromise that is a fair balance of interests through a true social partnership with the unions," Stumpfe said, using the vocabulary of consensus that had appeared all but lost as the dispute escalated.
But he warned on arrival in Frankfurt that the employers were not prepared to get a deal at any costs.
"If IG Metall does not want to discuss an overall package, then the top-level talks are over," Stumpfe said.

Gesamtmetall said earlier that it wanted to include discussion on sick-pay cuts as part of an overall negotiation on other worker benefits such as holiday and Christmas pay. -- Frankfurt Newsroom + 49 69 756525
